A Dance Dance Revolution cabinet showed up in the driveway. This is the start of the [personal series](../) — five notes on getting an arcade machine into the house and then slowly making it mine.

## Delivery day

The cab arrived on a pallet, wrapped like it had survived a few extra moves. Getting it off the truck was the whole event: two people, a furniture dolly, and a very honest conversation about door frames. The 573 hardware and the original monitor were still in the box, which is both the charm and the liability of buying a working machine instead of a pile of parts.

I checked the obvious things before we even wheeled it inside: no cracked marquee, pads that still had some life, and a power cable that wasn't a fire hazard. Everything else could wait until it was upright and plugged in.

## Unpacking

Once it was in the room, I cut the wrap, pulled the foam, and laid the hardware out so I could see what I actually owned. Cabinet, pad assembly, power brick, extra bolts, and a small bag of "you'll need these later" screws. I took photos of cable routing before I disconnected anything. Future me would thank present me for that.

The pads came off so we could get the cab through the last doorway. That turned a one-step move into a three-step move, but it also meant I got a first look at the underside of the stage. Dust, a few tired treads, and nothing that looked immediately broken.

## Assembly and setup

Reassembly was slower than the move. Pads back on, marquee seated, IO cables traced back to the 573, then the first power-on. Attract mode came up. The pads registered. The CRT needed a minute to settle. That was enough for day one.

I left the original mix on the machine and played a few songs to confirm the cabinet was actually a cabinet, not a very large paperweight. The upgrades — software, display, pads, and eventually the 573 itself — are the rest of this series.
